title: The Peal imperfect and imperative

objectives.can: Recognise Peal imperfects and imperatives and parse them.

explanation.summary: The Aramaic imperfect is built with a prefix in front of the stem: it is the form for what is not yet complete, such as what will happen, what may or should happen, and what is wished for. The imperative is the form of a command. This lesson teaches the prefixes, the plural endings and the few forms of each that the texts actually contain.

sections.heading: The imperfect: a prefix and sometimes an ending
body: The perfect of the last lesson put its endings after the stem. The imperfect works the other way round. A prefix goes in front of the stem and shows the person, and the plural, and the second person feminine, add an ending as well. The prefixes are י- for the third person, ת- for the second person (and also for the third person feminine), א- for the first person singular and נ- for the first person plural. Because ת- begins both a second-person and a third-person feminine singular, such a form is told from its neighbours: a 'she' in the sentence, or a 'you' being addressed.

The perfect tells what has been done, as a whole. The imperfect is used more widely: it often looks forward ('he will say'), it can say what happens regularly or what is possible, and in a sentence about a wish or a command it can have the sense of 'let him say' or 'may it be'. As with the perfect, the English rendering depends on the sentence. A good example is יֵאמַר in Daniel 2:7, where the Chaldeans say to the king: 'let the king tell the dream'.

sections.heading: The plural endings: -וּן, not -וּ
body: The plural of the imperfect ends in a long vowel and a final nun: -וּן for the masculine, -ָן for the feminine. This is one of the plainest differences between Aramaic and Hebrew, whose plural imperfect usually ends in a vowel with no nun. In the Aramaic of the Bible the nun is nearly always there: יִפְלְחוּן 'they will serve', תִּפְּלוּן 'you (plural) will fall'.

There is an exception that is worth knowing. In Jeremiah 10:11 the word יֵאבַדוּ 'they shall perish' has no final nun, and it is a plural. Grammarians describe such a short form as a jussive, the form of a wish or a command, and a few of the forms in these texts are read in that way. The texts have so few that the rule cannot be learned from them alone, so treat the missing nun as a signal and not as a rule.

sections.heading: The verb 'to be' and its prefix ל-
body: The third person of the verb הָוָא ('be, become') is written with ל- in place of י-: לֶהֱוֵא 'let it be', לֶהֱוֺן 'let them be'. This is a peculiarity of this verb. It is common in the texts, and it most often appears in wishes and commands, such as לֶהֱוֵא in Daniel 3:18, 'let it be known to you'. In the second person and the feminine the ordinary prefix ת- is kept: תֶּהֱוֵא 'she will be'.
The feminine plural of this verb is rare: לֶהֶוְיָן in Daniel 5:17 is the only one in the texts, and it has the ל- prefix and the ending -ָן.

sections.heading: The imperative
body: The imperative is used only for the second person, and it is made from the imperfect stem without the prefix. The masculine singular is the bare stem: אֱמַר 'say!', הַב 'give!', דַּע 'know!'. The plural masculine adds -וּ: אֱמַרוּ 'say!', שִׂימוּ 'set!'. The feminine singular adds -י: קוּמִי 'arise!'. The feminine plural does not occur in the texts. The table gives what the texts hold.

A command can be a courtesy as well as an order. In Daniel 2:4 the Chaldeans address the king with חֱיִי, 'live!': 'O king, live for ever!' The same greeting stands in Daniel 3:9, 5:10 and 6:7. It is a wish, and the imperative need not be read as a rude order.

misunderstandings: Do not read the imperfect as a future tense. It often points to the future, but it is also the form for a wish, a command and a regular event, and the sentence decides.
A prefix ת- can mean 'you' or 'she'. Both exist, and only the sentence shows which. Check the endings: -וּן with ת- is 'you (plural)', never 'she'.
Do not look for a Hebrew pattern. The Hebrew imperfect has no final nun in the plural; the Aramaic one has. A grammar of Hebrew will not describe these forms.
A missing nun is not a mistake. A plural without a final nun, as in יֵאבַדוּ, is a short form that some grammarians call a jussive. It is unusual and does not occur often.

deeper.heading: Why the verb 'to be' has ל-
body: Grammarians do not agree on where the ל- of the third person of הָוָא comes from. Some connect it with a particle of wishing, others with a sound change that affected this verb, and the question is not settled. For the learner the useful fact is only that ל- is the regular third-person prefix of this verb in the texts.

examples.analysis: חֱיִי (2) and אֱמַר (3) are both Peal imperatives, second person masculine singular. The first is the courtesy of the greeting, 'live!'. The second is a request in the form of a command, 'tell!', and its object is the dream. The imperative is the bare stem, so a good test is to look for the same stem inside the imperfect: אֱמַר is the stem of יֵאמַר in the next verses.

examples.analysis: יֵאמַר is a Peal imperfect, third person masculine singular, with the י- prefix. The subject is the king: the courtiers ask him, 'let him tell'. The imperfect is in a polite request addressed to a third person, as one speaks to a king. It has no final nun, since it is singular.
